stories.title: Mary Wollstonecraft's Struggle
stories.description: Amit recounts the life of Mary Wollstonecraft, a proto-feminist born in 1759. She faced a brutal patriarchal society where women had no rights. She wrote 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman', was called a 'hyena in petticoats', and attempted suicide by jumping into the Thames. She died of childbed fever after giving birth to Mary Shelley, leaving a legacy of radical thought.

stories.title: The Birth of Frankenstein
stories.description: Amit tells the story of 18-year-old Mary Shelley, who ran away with Percy Shelley. In 1816, during a gathering with Lord Byron and others, she wrote 'Frankenstein' as part of a ghost story contest. She invented the science fiction genre without any models, exploring deep questions about creation and responsibility.

stories.title: Semmelweis and Handwashing
stories.description: Ajay shares the tragic story of Ignaz Semmelweis, who discovered that handwashing could prevent childbed fever in maternity wards. Despite dropping mortality rates from 18% to near zero, he was ridiculed by the medical establishment because his ideas contradicted prevailing theories (and class norms). He died in a lunatic asylum, possibly after being beaten.

stories.title: Alfred Wegener's Continental Drift
stories.description: Ajay discusses Alfred Wegener, who proposed continental drift in 1912 after noticing the fit between Africa and South America. He was mocked for lacking a mechanism and died in Greenland before his theory was accepted as plate tectonics in the 1960s.

stories.title: Darwin's Delay
stories.description: Ajay recounts how Charles Darwin sat on his theory of evolution for over 20 years, terrified of the backlash. He only published 'On the Origin of Species' after Alfred Russel Wallace independently discovered the same theory while suffering from malaria in Indonesia.

recommendations.comment: Amit recommends this dual biography by Charlotte Gordon, which tells the interlocking stories of Mary Wollstonecraft and Mary Shelley.

recommendations.item: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
recommendations.comment: Amit recommends Mary Wollstonecraft's seminal feminist work, noting that while some parts may seem tame today, it was radically ahead of its time.
Amit recommends Mary Shelley's masterpiece, not just as a horror story but as a profound work of science fiction dealing with AI ethics and the nature of life.
Ajay recommends Jacob Bronowski's book (and TV series) for its coverage of scientific history, including the story of Boltzmann.
Amit recommends this book by Chinmay Tumbe for its accounts of historical pandemics and the resistance to scientific insights like those of John Snow.

Amit recommends this essay by Paul Graham, which categorizes people into conventional/independent and passive/aggressive, arguing that the 'aggressively conventional-minded' are the enemies of progress.

recommendations.item: Who's Got the Guts to Go to the Moon?
recommendations.comment: Amit recommends this essay by Adam Mastroianni, which argues that modern science has become too safe and bureaucratic, discouraging 'moonshots'.

core_ideas.description: True innovation often comes from 'outlaws'—people who are socially maladjusted, weird, or willing to break norms. The very quality that makes them 'weird' allows them to see truths that others miss.

The biggest barrier to progress is not ignorance but the 'aggressively conventional-minded'—people who actively police the boundaries of acceptable thought and attack new ideas to signal tribal loyalty.

Listening to mavericks is an arbitrage opportunity (a '$500 bill on the ground'). It is in our self-interest to seek out and listen to 'mad people' because they might be right about the next big thing.

Modern institutions (academia, grants) select for conscientiousness and conformity ('clean shirt', 'one of the boys'). This filters out the creative geniuses who are often difficult or unconventional.
Science advances one funeral at a time. New truths are rarely accepted by convincing opponents; rather, the opponents eventually die, and a new generation grows up familiar with the truth.
